item.title: The Digital Recovery Paradox: How Habitual Smartphone Use Relates to Psychological Recovery
item.dc:creator: Hongxing Meng, Jinhua Gan, Xinran Peng, Hui Ma, Hanying Tang
item.description:
Media Psychology · Hongxing Meng, Jinhua Gan, Xinran Peng, Hui Ma, Hanying Tang

Topics: Digital well-being, Smartphone use, Mental health, Longitudinal study

Although smartphones are frequently used for post-work recovery, their restorative value remains contested. Integrating the Proactive Recovery Dual-Pathway Framework with habit theory, this research investigates how habitual smartphone use (HSU) relates differently to avoidance- and approach-oriented recovery. In Study 1, using a two-wave survey of 309 full-time employees in China, Bayesian network structure learning mapped the multivariate recovery ecosystem. Results revealed that while HSU facilitates avoidance-oriented recovery (psychological detachment), it structurally crowds out resource-building experiences (mastery), operating as a behavioral strategy with potential opportunity costs. Study 2, a four-week randomized field experiment with Chinese employees (final N = 110), tested an implementation-intention intervention against an active psychoeducational control. While “if-then” plans effectively curtailed HSU – demonstrating the modifiability of automated digital habits – this reduction did not spontaneously translate into enhanced proactive recovery or work vigor. Together, these findings clarify the digital recovery paradox by theoretically distinguishing between habit cessation and resource accumulation. We conclude that neutralizing passive smartphone consumption is insufficient on its own; achieving true digital well-being requires explicitly coupling habit-reduction strategies with the intentional reallocation of time toward mastery-oriented pursuits.

item.title: Financial journalists’ expertise: The JCK tango of journalism and economics
item.dc:creator: Hagar Lahav, Zvi Reich, Liri Blum
item.description:
Journalism · Hagar Lahav, Zvi Reich, Liri Blum

Topics: Journalism studies, Journalistic practice, Journalism, Professional identity

This paper examines economic journalists’ expertise by integrating a theoretical model, Journalistic Content Knowledge (JCK), with a new research method, News Sorting. JCK proposes that beat journalists’ expertise lies in the merger of domain-specific knowledge and journalistic know-how. News Sorting tests this proposition by having journalists rank both subject-matter and journalistic challenges they encountered in producing samples of their publications. Based on News Sorting sessions in which 20 Israeli financial journalists ranked 498 items, the study reveals how economic and journalistic knowledge interact in specific cases of economic reporting. The findings show that JCK operates slightly asymmetrically in economic news: economic challenges are somewhat higher than journalistic ones, especially in items involving macroeconomics, finance, taxation, and intersections between economics, politics, and law. Rather than forming a single, homogeneous expertise, economic journalists’ expertise takes shape around three epistemic orientations that prioritize information gathering, news analysis, or the clear presentation of economic information.

item.title: Between perception and practice: Audience understandings of journalistic impartiality and broadcast regulation
item.dc:creator: Kathryn J. Perkins, Stephen Cushion, Maxwell Modell, Matt Walsh
item.description:
Journalism · Kathryn J. Perkins, Stephen Cushion, Maxwell Modell, Matt Walsh

Topics: Media trust, Journalism, Media framing, Media systems

This article examines public complaints about impartiality in the UK and audience (mis)understandings of how the regulator, Ofcom, enforces it. We explore an issue often neglected in studies of media governance: how closely do public expectations of impartial journalism align with how it is applied by a regulator? We adopt a comprehensive mixed-methods approach by drawing on a nationally representative survey of 2,153 UK adults, a systematic analysis of complaints to Ofcom in 2025 ( n = 47,457 complaints), and four focus groups. Our analysis of complaints to Ofcom revealed audience concerns were concentrated on a small number of high-profile cases, while formal findings against broadcasters, particularly for impartiality, were exceptionally rare. The audience findings revealed a substantial gap between public expectations and regulatory practice, with most people overestimating how often broadcasters breached impartiality rules and expressing confusion around why regulation was not more robust. The article argues that public concern about journalistic bias is shaped less by regulatory outcomes than by experiential judgements about news coverage. More broadly, the study makes an original contribution to debates about a growing mistrust in news media by revealing that misunderstandings of regulation are undermining public confidence and faith in impartial journalism.

item.title: News Frames and Online Political Hostility: Evidence from the 2022 South Korean Presidential Election
item.dc:creator: Hyo-sun Ryu, Jae Kook Lee
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Hyo-sun Ryu, Jae Kook Lee

Topics: News framing, Political polarization, Computational text analysis, Election campaigns

This study examines the relationship between election news frames and online political hostility using approximately 200,000 news stories and 24 million comments from the 2022 South Korean presidential election. Applying computational text analysis and a deep learning model, we categorized news frames into strategy and issue frames and analyzed their associations with political hostility and incitement to hostility in comments. Results show that strategy frames are associated with higher rates of both, with candidate-centered coverage showing stronger associations than horse-race coverage. Implications of these results are discussed.

item.title: Understanding discursive constructions of violence in online incel communities
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth A. Hintz, Nolan Bowers, Jonathan Baker, Timothy Betts
item.description:
Communication Monographs · Elizabeth A. Hintz, Nolan Bowers, Jonathan Baker, Timothy Betts

Topics: Online communities, Social media discourse, Violence, Content analysis

Understanding how involuntarily celibates (“incels”) discuss violence online is essential for preventing violence. Guided by relational dialectics theory (RDT), we analyze online incel communities to illuminate how discourses animate meanings about violence. We identify three discourses, six dialogically contractive discursive practices, one form of diachronic separation, and three forms of synchronic interplay. We advance RDT by: (a) theorizing meta-discourses as recursive organizing logics across distal and proximal links, (b) conceptualizing discourses as agentic forces operating across extended utterance chains, (c) examining how triadic interplay contributes to resistance and the premature meaning finalization, (d) reconceptualizing the carnivalesque as a site of durable discursive closure, and (e) introducing dialogic “elasticity” to account for variation in the susceptibility of semantic objects to transformation.

item.title: Theories and models predicting communication channel selection: a scoping review and synthesis
item.dc:creator: Matthew R. Erxleben, Jesse Fox
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Matthew R. Erxleben, Jesse Fox

Topics: Communication theory, Interpersonal communication, Computer-mediated communication, Communication research

Abstract As communication technologies continue to diversify our media environment, it is critical to understand how and why individuals select certain channels to communicate with others (e.g., face-to-face [FtF], texting, videoconferencing). First, we provide a clear conceptualization of channel selection to distinguish it from other constructs (e.g., media selection, technology adoption). Following PRISMA guidelines, we then conducted an interdisciplinary scoping review of theories and models related to channel and media choice, reviewing 4,843 sources. We identified 73 distinct theories, models, and frameworks in our initial process. Among these, we identified 38 theories that explicitly elaborated the process of individuals’ channel selection (rather than processes such as media content selection, media planning, technology adoption, or media use) and coded their primary foci and areas of origin (e.g., organizational communication, mass communication). We offer a retrospective narrative review briefly describing each channel selection theory contextualized within their theoretical predecessors (e.g., social presence theory, uses and gratifications, diffusion of innovations). Our synthesis offers additional insights on the strengths and weaknesses of current theorizing, suggesting directions for future research. Notable deficits include a lack of explication regarding how people select multiple channels, particularly over time, and a limited number of theories derived from interpersonal communication.

item.title: Gendered personalization in economic news media coverage: Analyzing the presentation of female and male CEOs
item.dc:creator: Sarah Marschlich, Nora Denner
item.description:
Journalism · Sarah Marschlich, Nora Denner

Topics: Gender representation, News framing, Personalization, Content analysis

This paper takes a gender perspective on personalization, i.e., the shift in media portrayals from institutions to individual actors, in the media coverage of Chief Executive Officers (CEOs). Using mediatization, social role, and role congruity theories, we examine gendered personalization in U.S. newspaper reporting. A quantitative content analysis of 304 articles from The New York Times and USA Today published between January 2023 and December 2024, covering 20 Fortune 500 CEOs (10 women and 10 men), yielded 331 mentions of CEOs. Our findings reveal that male CEOs appear slightly more frequently in the news and that reporting on them emphasizes external, strategic, and political issues, while female CEOs are more often linked to internal, people-oriented topics, such as management and human resources. Both genders are primarily portrayed in professional contexts, with few references to their private lives or appearances. Furthermore, we found that companies with female CEOs are evaluated more negatively than those with male CEOs, suggesting a negativity bias against female-led companies. Overall, our study indicates that traditional gendered coverage persists in business news. At the same time, the absence of overt gender-based personalization suggests a more professionalized portrayal of corporate leadership in business news today; however, given the cross-sectional design, this remains indicative rather than conclusive.

item.title: When to be tough and when to be tender: Source cultivation tradecraft among award-winning Canadian investigative journalists
item.dc:creator: Chris Arsenault
item.description:
Journalism · Chris Arsenault

Topics: Investigative journalism, Journalistic practice, Journalism, Source protection

Investigative journalists depend on human sources, yet the sustained work of building and protecting those relationships has received less scholarly attention than its centrality to the craft would suggest. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 17 award-winning Canadian investigative journalists, conducted on the record and named with consent, this study examines how elite reporters cultivate, verify and safeguard sources. Six themes describe source cultivation as an integrated tradecraft rather than a discrete skill: tacit knowledge as an engine of access, an asymmetric ethics of toughness and care, triangulation architectures for credibility, cultivation as slow journalism, source protection as embedded practice, and the interplay of public records and human sources. Two contributions extend existing scholarship. First, participants apply ethical obligations asymmetrically, sorting sources by relative power and treating care as a structuring logic that runs through interview design and publication decisions. Second, documentary and human sourcing operate as functionally inseparable rather than parallel evidentiary streams. Points of divergence within the cohort are also documented.

item.title: Journalistic deception: Exploring the relationship between propaganda, disinformation, and independent journalism in an authoritarian regime
item.dc:creator: Nicole Marie Klevanskaya
item.description:
Journalism · Nicole Marie Klevanskaya

Topics: Propaganda, Disinformation, Journalism, Authoritarian media systems

A newer line of scholarship urges researchers to devote more attention to “propaganda-press cultures,” which are defined as media environments in which journalists participate in or challenge propaganda. In such environments, propaganda and journalism become increasingly intertwined. Drawing on a visual and textual analysis of 174 online news articles, this study examines Russian exiled journalists’ role in the propaganda-press culture that has arisen out of the war in Ukraine. Findings reveal that Russian exiled journalists subvert, resist, and actively refute Russian propaganda narratives. However, at the same time, they also inadvertently give leverage to propaganda by (1) presenting alternative explanations for events and (2) sharing stories that indirectly provide legitimacy to Russian propaganda. In addition to expanding understandings of propaganda-press cultures beyond the West, this study points toward the complexities of authoritarian media systems by highlighting the more covert ways in which exiled journalists can engage with deception.

item.title: Taking a political stance: Representations of the health of American democracy and the women’s suffrage movement in U.S. Vogue ’s editorials (1892–1918)
item.dc:creator: Chrysi Dagoula
item.description:
Journalism · Chrysi Dagoula

Topics: Political communication, Media framing, Content analysis, Journalism history

The dominant view of Vogue is that it is, as a cultural fashion icon, somewhat a-political, focusing on matters of style, beauty, culture, lifestyle, and runway. And yet this is not the case. As this study proves, from the very beginning, Vogue was deeply engaged with politics and the related issues of social policy. Not in an ideological way but more pragmatically so. As such, the political outlook of the editorials during the period 1892-1918, which is the focus of this paper, spans seven identifiable political themes: the health of democracy; women’s rights and women’s suffrage; social class; race; foreign affairs; religion; and social policy issues. Identifying these themes allows to understand the multivocality of Vogue’s political outlook. Sometimes a voice of progress and sometimes a voice of conservatism, sometimes an outlook that is inspiring and sometimes an outlook that is troubling. This study focuses on two of these themes, the health of democracy and the rights and role of women more generally (including the women’s suffrage movement). Through a thematic and a structural-hermeneutic analysis of 1109 editorials, the paper examines their underlying binary structure and their political messaging and meaning.

item.title: Rethinking the Role of Journalism in the Open-Source Intelligence Ecosystem: Inside the Data Pipeline of Cross-Border Investigative Journalism Hubs
item.dc:creator: Lindita Camaj
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Lindita Camaj

Topics: Investigative journalism, Journalism, Digital journalism, Data journalism

Cross-border investigative journalism increasingly operates through a journalism-commons logic that integrates open-source intelligence (OSINT) practices into shared digital infrastructures. This paper examines investigative platforms built by five prominent global and regional cross-border hubs (OCCRP, ICIJ, ARIJ, CLIP, and Code for Africa) to analyze how their technical design enacts the journalism-commons logic across technological, social, and content layers. Using a comparative case-study approach informed by knowledge management systems (KMS) theory, the analysis identifies an infrastructure typology that ranges from document-centric collaboration tools to entity-centric repositories and decentralized connectors, revealing three modes of knowledge sharing: technological, content-driven, and hybrid. By tracing how each organization balances openness, security, and long-term sustainability, the paper emphasizes implications of public-records mining under divergent political and socio-cultural conditions for asymmetric dependencies between the Global North and the Majority World.

item.title: Driven by Politics? Comparative Evidence on Journalists’ Perceived Political Influences Over Time
item.dc:creator: Pauline Zecchinon, Olivier Standaert, Thomas Hanitzsch, Folker Hanusch, Imke Henkel, Sandra Lábová, Vera Slavtcheva‐Petkova
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Pauline Zecchinon, Olivier Standaert, Thomas Hanitzsch, Folker Hanusch, Imke Henkel, Sandra Lábová, Vera Slavtcheva‐Petkova

Topics: Journalistic roles, Press freedom, Political influence, Comparative research

This study explored how journalists’ perceptions of political influences altered over nearly a decade, between the mid-2010s and the mid-2020s, using comparative data from 54 countries collected in two waves of the Worlds of Journalism Study and data assessing the political contexts of these countries. To interpret the temporal dynamics, we proposed a “filter model” that links the broader political context to perceived political influences through successive stages, each of which can dampen, redirect or override systemic factors. Examining the interplay between political influences and external political developments, the study showed that journalists’ perceptions were consistently related to indicators of democratic performance, underscoring the importance of national and regional contextual factors that shape journalistic cultures. Rather than a universal increase or decrease, perceived political influences evolved unevenly across countries. These uneven trajectories correlated with changes in democracy measures, such as the Freedom in the World index, although less strongly than expected. This pattern is consistent with the filter model: organisational structures, journalistic practices and routines and individual perspectives can absorb, redirect or even mask changes in the political environment, so that journalists’ perceptions do not simply mirror the changes in political realities.

item.title: Incompatible Interpretive Worlds: TikTok, Douyin, and Geopolitical Narratives of the Russia–Ukraine War
item.dc:creator: Jing Yang, Zhiyuan Liang
item.description:
Media and Communication · Jing Yang, Zhiyuan Liang

Topics: TikTok, Digital platforms, Political communication, Platform governance

This study compares the ways TikTok and its mainland Chinese counterpart, Douyin, have mediated the Russia–Ukraine war, generating divergent geopolitical narratives. It examines the political role of platform dissemination in contemporary warfare by analysing how platform logics and governance contexts shape public sense-making of conflict. On TikTok, war narratives emerge through creator-led circulation, cross-border viewing, translation, and comment-mediated interpretation, producing forms of transnational witnessing that are affective, participatory, and contested. In contrast, Douyin operates within the Chinese domestic discourse system, where official emphasis on neutrality, stability, and diplomatic restraint shapes its dominant interpretive framework. In the corpus, footage of frontline violence appears less consistently prominent, while explanatory narratives attributing the war to NATO expansion or Western provocation appear frequently in high-visibility content. This distribution should not be interpreted as an explicit pro-Russian diplomatic stance. Rather, it reflects the importance of sovereignty-oriented reasoning and nationalist sentiment in Chinese political communication. Drawing on comparative qualitative content analysis of high-engagement, platform-curated war-related videos retrieved through hashtag-based sampling on TikTok and Douyin, this study argues that the two applications produce incompatible interpretive worlds: one organised around transnational humanitarian witnessing and contested moral interpretation, and the other around institutionally anchored geopolitical explanation, sovereignty-oriented reasoning, and participatory nationalist uptake.

item.title: “Burnout with shrapnel.” The influence of perceived supervisor and organizational support on worker burnout and retention in U.S. local television newsrooms
item.dc:creator: Carey L. Higgins-Dobney
item.description:
Journalism · Carey L. Higgins-Dobney

Topics: Journalism, News production, Newsroom practices, Well-being

Employee burnout and high turnover rates are growing concerns in local television newsrooms in the United States. This study uses the framework of Organizational Support Theory (OST) to examine how Perceived Organizational Support (POS) and Perceived Supervisor Support (PSS) impact the overall work experiences of U.S. local television news employees. Interviews with 21 of these workers describe working conditions, including stress, mental health, burnout and future plans in the industry. Most workers describe low levels of both PSS and POS and highlight a noticeable gap between what they feel they need to succeed in their jobs and what many organizations and supervisors can – or perhaps want to – provide. Those that have higher PSS and/or POS describe stronger levels of mentorship and mental health support and lower levels of turnover in their newsrooms. Participants provide practical suggestions to help alleviate some of the more negative aspects of the job contributing to burnout and provide incentives to remain in the business.

item.title: Public funding of private media: How perceived work environment and journalistic roles explain support for public policies
item.dc:creator: Elsa Costa e Silva
item.description:
Journalism · Elsa Costa e Silva

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic roles, Media systems, Public opinion

Public funding of private media has a long tradition in Europe and, in face of the dying traditional business models, there is an increasing demand for such mechanism in several democratic contexts. Portugal has not, until now, a national public policy to support private companies, nor, for instance, a tradition of media subsidies. However, due to the financial struggles of most media companies, the topic is hot on the agenda. This paper examines Portuguese journalists’ views on public funding of private media. While the issue of public funding has been widely discussed in the public sphere, the support of professionals for such a public policy has not yet been widely studied. Based on a survey of 280 journalists, this study shows significant support for public funding of private companies. This support is associated with journalists’ work environment, such as perceptions of their employer’s financial and economic conditions or the type of media organization (public, private, non-profit), but not with self-perceived precarity. Different journalistic roles are also related to support for public funding: professionals who subscribe to a more adversarial role refuse public funding, whereas journalists who align more with the dissemination function support it.

item.title: Affordances-based resistance to digital surveillance
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Caliandro, Ilir Rama, Veronica Moretti
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Alessandro Caliandro, Ilir Rama, Veronica Moretti

Topics: Digital surveillance, Platform affordances, Social media discourse, Computational text analysis

This article introduces the notion of affordances-based resistance to digital surveillance as a practice mediated by the socio-technical architecture of digital platforms: a type of countersurveillance that is not organised or structured by the norms and practices of social and political movements, but is instead structured and held together by the technical features of digital media and the participatory cultures thriving on them. Specifically, we consider this resistance passive and mechanical because it is: driven by the affordances (and not resulting from an active manipulation of them); individualised and dispersed on a large scale, not localised in or governed by traditional social organisations (e.g. civic associations); and a form of resistance in which actors are more nudged towards resistance behaviours than deliberately pursuing them. To illustrate, we develop a cross-platform analysis of Twitter and the Google Play Store, examining 270,656 tweets and 23,469 reviews about the contact tracing app Immuni. The article contributes by introducing a novel concept for studying resistance to datafication and by proposing a methodological approach linking low- and high-level affordances through cross-platform analysis.

item.title: Which Is the Antecedent: Loneliness or Problematic Mobile Phone Use? Evidence from the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model and Cross-Lagged Panel Network Analysis
item.dc:creator: Mengmeng Zhang, Xiantong Yang
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Mengmeng Zhang, Xiantong Yang

Topics: Loneliness, Problematic mobile phone use, Mobile media, Adolescent mental health

Despite growing evidence linking loneliness with problematic mobile phone use (PMPU), the temporal direction between these constructs remains debated. Drawing on the cognitive-behavioral model of pathological Internet use and the compensatory Internet use theory, loneliness is theorized to increase PMPU as a coping strategy for social isolation, whereas the displacement hypothesis suggests that PMPU may instead serve as an antecedent of loneliness. To resolve this theoretical inconsistency, we examined both variable- and symptom-level associations between loneliness and PMPU using the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) and cross-lagged panel network analysis (CLPN). A total of 768 adolescents completed three assessments at approximately 6-month intervals over 1 year. The RI-CLPM revealed bidirectional within-person associations: higher loneliness predicted greater subsequent PMPU, and elevated PMPU predicted increased loneliness over time. The CLPN further uncovered the strongest cross-lagged edges were all from loneliness to PMPU symptoms. Additionally, several key nodes in the network were identified. From T1 to T2, PMPU5 ( friends/family complaint ) showed the highest out-EI and PMPU9 ( excessive duration notification ) had the highest in-EI; from T2 to T3, PMPU6 ( unexpected usage duration ) showed the highest out-EI and PMPU4 ( mobile check anxiety ) had the highest in-EI. These findings highlight the importance of integrating variable- and symptom-level approaches to advance theoretical understanding of the dynamic association between loneliness and PMPU and to inform practical interventions that help break this vicious cycle among adolescents.

item.title: The transformation of interactive journalism through new media platforms in Kyrgyzstan
item.dc:creator: Aizhan Umarova, Venera Sabirova, Mahabbat Mamyrova, Chinara Abdieva, Jyrgal Sakybaeva
item.description:
Journalism · Aizhan Umarova, Venera Sabirova, Mahabbat Mamyrova, Chinara Abdieva, Jyrgal Sakybaeva

Topics: Interactive journalism, Digital journalism, New media, Multimedia storytelling

The aim of the research was to determine the role of independent means of transmitting, storing, and reproducing information in the media industry. The analysis of innovative formats of interactive content was conducted based on internet resources such as 24.kg, Kaktus.media, Factcheck.kg, International Budget Partnership, and April. The study examined video resources, interactive maps, infographics, and multimedia storytelling for creating reports and independent investigations. The research highlighted the influence of new media platforms on interactive journalism. The main difference between interactive journalism and traditional journalism was identified as the two-way communication process. It was noted that the popularity of new media is growing, offering new methods that differ from traditional forms of journalism. These include active interaction with users through chatbots, surveys, and more; the integration of audience participation (streams) and multimedia formats (video, photos, podcasts, infographics). The advantages of these media were identified as the rapid dissemination of information, global reach, cost minimisation, and multimedia content. The study also explored innovative formats of media journalism: interactive journalism, multimedia storytelling, data-driven journalism, journalism using artificial intelligence, social media journalism, journalism with augmented and virtual reality (VR), and gamified journalism. The analysis showed that new media platforms contribute to the functional transformation of journalism by expanding interactive formats and tools for two-way communication. However, the study does not claim to statistically measure audience growth, engagement rates, or trust levels; rather, it identifies the mechanisms through which Kyrgyz media create conditions for audience participation in interactive journalism.

item.title: Constructing European defence: From capability gaps to future trajectories in an IISS strategic dossier
item.dc:creator: Nuria Blanco Hernández
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Nuria Blanco Hernández

Topics: Strategic communication, Discourse analysis, Frame analysis, Science communication

Strategic documents produced by think tanks occupy an important communicative space between expert knowledge, institutional authority and public policy. This article examines how the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) constructs and legitimises the need to transform European defence in its 2025 strategic dossier, Progress and Shortfalls in Europe's Defence: An Assessment . Adopting a document-centred qualitative case study, the analysis combines critical discourse analysis, framing and discursive legitimation with complementary attention to argumentation, securitisation and strategic narratives. The dossier is analysed in its entirety, comprising 98 substantive pages, approximately 62,095 words and 440 unique identifiable sources. Qualitative coding identifies seven recurring discursive operations through which European defence is constructed as an urgent, measurable and relational strategic problem. The findings show how evidence, institutional and expert authority, urgency and feasibility are articulated to legitimate defence transformation. The article contributes to Communication and Media Studies by conceptualising the expert strategic document as a communicative site where strategic problems and future trajectories are constructed and legitimised.

item.title: ‘Like going out at night without pepper spray’: responses to cyber-victimization among LGBTQIA+college students in the United States
item.dc:creator: Paul Bleakley, Megan Trafford, Maya Maayani
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Paul Bleakley, Megan Trafford, Maya Maayani

Topics: Cyberbullying, Online harassment, Platform governance, Privacy

The internet has reshaped the nature of social interactions, providing new environments for people to connect in both prosocial and, too often, antisocial ways. The lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, questioning, intersex, asexual, and associated (LGBTQIA+) communities are among those who studies reveal are most at risk for cyber-victimization. For young people, already the most vulnerable to being targeted, being openly LGBTQIA + serves to compound the likelihood of online harassment. This study reports on three focus groups conducted with LGBTQIA + college students at a mid-sized university in the United States northeast, who discussed their experiences with cyber-victimization. The findings indicate a lack of faith in systemic platform-based responses, and a consensus that young LGBTQIA + people are forced to take personal responsibility for their own online safety. This includes curating their online profiles and feeds, as well as (to a lesser extent) taking direct action to combat anti-LGBTQIA + abuse.

item.title: Building the Open-Source Investigation Tools of the Future: Why Collaboration is Key
item.dc:creator: Johanna Wild
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Johanna Wild

Topics: Open-source intelligence, Digital investigation, Digital literacy, Journalism

Whenever we hold a workshop or talk with aspiring open-source researchers at conferences, there is one type of question that comes up time and again: “What are the best tools right now?” or “What tools should I learn first?” Beginners are often fixated on tools because to them, it can feel like knowing the right tools is synonymous with mastering open-source investigations. This is not the case. A clear research goal, creativity in finding dispersed online information in expected and unexpected places, and the tenacity to persist even when the research does not yield immediate results are more important than tools.

item.title: “We Tried to Warn You, but the Coal Mine’s on Fire Now”: The Adult Industry Trade Press as Advocacy Journalism
item.dc:creator: Chelsea Julian Reynolds
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Chelsea Julian Reynolds

Topics: Advocacy journalism, Journalism, Content moderation, Digital platforms

FOSTA/SESTA is an anti-sex trafficking law passed during the first Trump presidency. The bipartisan legislation was celebrated as a step toward online safety. Years later, the law has not made measurable impacts on the commercial sex trade or on child sexual exploitation. It has, however, created a chilling effect on sexual speech that now permeates digital spaces. This paper presents an analysis of 209 news stories about FOSTA/SESTA published in adult industry trade publications XBIZ and AVN, contrasting findings with earlier coverage in legacy newspapers and LGBT and feminist media. More than other outlets, adult industry trade media produced early, in-depth legal analysis that raised concerns about sexual censorship at the federal level. XBIZ and AVN covered FOSTA/SESTA’s impacts on sex workers, the tech industry, and creative sectors, focusing on Big Tech overreach and legislative threats to freedom of sexual expression. Workers rights were emphasized. Algorithmic surveillance, AI, and cryptocurrency were included in the editorial mix years before these topics became common in the legacy press. This study underscores the watchdog role of the adult industry trade press and theorizes it as a genre of advocacy journalism. Implications for journalism research and creator studies are discussed.

item.title: From exception to norm: Multilingual publics in North Africa and lessons for the theory of the public sphere
item.dc:creator: Valerian Thielicke
item.description:
Communication Theory · Valerian Thielicke

Topics: Communication theory, Media systems, Cross-cultural communication, Public opinion

Abstract Most societies and polities worldwide are multilingual, yet most theories of public spheres overlook this fact, as they stem from Western contexts dominated by a single national language. Reviewing the scientific literature, I show that multilingualism is often treated as a problem or exception rather than the norm. Drawing on four observations from publics in North Africa, I highlight insights relevant to general theories of public spheres: (1) the role of translation and coexistence of multiple languages within one public sphere; (2) the complex relationship between freedom of speech and language; (3) the correlation between language and levels of critique; and (4) the strategic potential of multilingualism. All point to the ambiguous role of language for publics. Finally, I propose a first draft of a theoretical framework for public spheres that recognizes multilingual realities, showing that existing theories contain elements that can integrate this global condition.

item.title: Presence, Social Capital, Social Isolation in Virtual Environments: The Role of Extraversion in Shaping Relational Outcomes
item.dc:creator: 김도현, Kyungmin Kim, Hun Kim
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · 김도현, Kyungmin Kim, Hun Kim

Topics: Virtual environments, Social presence, Social capital, Social isolation

Virtual environment communication has been increasingly discussed as a potential means of addressing social isolation, yet little is known about how different forms of presence become relational resources. This study examines how physical presence and social presence in virtual environments are associated with social isolation through virtual-environment bonding and bridging social capital, and whether these relationships differ by users' level of extraversion. Data were collected from 500 Korean adults with experience using ZEPETO and analyzed using CB-SEM and multi-group analysis. The results show that physical presence is positively associated with both bonding and bridging social capital, suggesting that perceived realism is associated with both forms of relational resources. Social presence is negatively associated with bonding social capital but positively associated with bridging social capital, indicating that the sense of being with others may be more closely associated with weak-tie expansion rather than close relational cohesion. Bonding social capital is positively associated with social isolation, whereas bridging social capital is not significantly associated with social isolation in the overall model. Multi-group analysis revealed that the positive association between bonding social capital and social isolation was significantly stronger among extraverted users. Bridging social capital was negatively associated with social isolation only in the extraversion group, although the between-group difference was not statistically significant at the 0.05 level. These findings suggest that the socio-psychological outcomes associated with VE-Comm vary not simply on the overall level of presence, but on the type of presence, the form of social capital reported, and users' personality traits.

item.title: Contesting unity: Media representations of national identity in Malaysia’s multilingual press
item.dc:creator: Yang Lai Fong
item.description:
Journalism · Yang Lai Fong

Topics: Media framing, National identity, Content analysis, Political communication

This study examined how four selected Malaysian news outlets represented national identity in a multicultural and politically contested society. Drawing on framing theory and Ariely’s (2019) conceptualization of national identity, it analyzed 104 articles published in 2024 by Harian Metro (Malay), Sin Chew Daily (Chinese), The Star (English), and the English-language edition of the digital-native outlet Malaysiakini . The content analysis examined reporting volume, article types, news sources, frames, and tones. Sin Chew contributed the most coverage, while political actors were the dominant sources across all four outlets. “Interethnic harmony, multiculturalism, and diversity” constituted the dominant frame across most outlets, but ethnic tensions and competing interpretations of nationhood persisted. Other frames included the “defense of Malay identity”, “racism against non-Malays”, and “East Malaysia’s marginalization”. Coverage in Harian Metro and The Star was predominantly inclusive, whereas Malaysiakini gave comparatively greater visibility to contestation and democratic deliberation. The findings show that the coverage represented Malaysian national identity as a dynamic and continuously negotiated process. The observed patterns are consistent with differences in the outlets’ linguistic audiences and institutional positions and can be interpreted within the context of Malaysia’s nation-building legacies. The study contributes to framing research by documenting systematic variation across selected legacy and digital-native outlets within the same multilingual media environment.

item.title: Can solutions journalism counter news avoidance? A choice experiment examining effects on emotions, self-efficacy, and news engagement
item.dc:creator: Kim Viborg Andersen, Monika Djerf‐Pierre, Adam Shehata, Maria Zuiderveld, Christina Åhrén
item.description:
Journalism · Kim Viborg Andersen, Monika Djerf‐Pierre, Adam Shehata, Maria Zuiderveld, Christina Åhrén

Topics: Journalism, News avoidance, Solutions journalism, Media effects

Solutions journalism has been proposed as a potential remedy to the negativity bias in news coverage, which is often blamed for emotional exhaustion and disengagement among audiences, eventually leading to news avoidance. However, it remains unclear who is drawn to such content and what effects it produces. This study presents a large-scale choice experiment ( N = 4622) examining preferences for solution-focused versus problem-focused journalism on antibiotic resistance, and the effects on emotions, self-efficacy, and news engagement. Participants were presented with one of four news stories focused on either problems or solutions at either an individual level or societal level. Some participants were assigned to watch a specific news story, and others were free to choose themselves. The results show a clear preference for solutions journalism, particularly when stories are framed at the individual level, though not more strongly among news avoiders. Exposure to solutions journalism increases positive emotions, reduces negative ones, and enhances self-efficacy, but does not boost news engagement (e.g., sharing, searching, or discussion). Together, the findings suggest that solutions journalism can to some extent counter news avoidance, yet it is not a definitive remedy.

item.title: One election, multiple stories: Polarized visual framing and media bias in the 2024 Turkish Mayoral elections
item.dc:creator: Gіzem Melek, Öykü Yenen Aytekin, Deniz Özyurda-Ergen
item.description:
Journalism · Gіzem Melek, Öykü Yenen Aytekin, Deniz Özyurda-Ergen

Topics: Political polarization, Media bias, Media framing, Election campaigns

This study examines visual framing and media bias during Türkiye’s 2024 mayoral elections, a pivotal contest that marked the ruling AKP’s most significant electoral defeat in two decades. It investigates whether patterns of polarization identified in textual coverage extend to visual framing within a highly polarized media system operating under a competitive authoritarian regime. The analysis draws on a dataset of 6926 visuals published during the official campaign period on the websites of 11 legacy and alternative news outlets, covering six major mayoral candidates in İstanbul, Ankara, and İzmir. Using systematic content analysis, the study codes Grabe and Bucy’s visual character framing, and determines disparities in candidate portrayal and visibility across outlets with different political orientations. The findings reveal pronounced asymmetries between pro-government and pro-opposition media in both tone and volume of coverage. Pro-government outlets grant ruling-party candidates greater visibility and more favorable portrayals, while opposition candidates receive comparatively limited or strategically unfavorable framing. These results demonstrate that visual bias operates not only through framing choices but also through systematic exposure inequalities. The study argues that visual framing reinforces polarization and ruling-party advantage, contributing to the reproduction of uneven political competition in competitive authoritarian regimes.

item.title: Normative ideals and empirical realities: Viewpoint diversity in the discourse on German arms deliveries to Ukraine
item.dc:creator: Laura Liebig, Gregor Wiedemann, Katharina Kleinen-von Königslöw
item.description:
Journalism · Laura Liebig, Gregor Wiedemann, Katharina Kleinen-von Königslöw

Topics: Media bias, News coverage, Machine learning, Political communication

Criticism of media coverage is an essential democratic mechanism to hold journalism accountable, yet it can also foster distrust and perceptions of media bias. This study examines such tensions through the case of the German media discourse on arms deliveries to Ukraine. Using accusations of one-sided reporting as a starting point, we theorize normative expectations of media diversity in war-related policy discourse and empirically assess how leading German news outlets represented competing viewpoints. Drawing on a two-year corpus (2022-2023) from 14 Leitmedien and employing a hierarchical supervised machine-learning approach based on (large) language models, we classify stances and frames to compute standard diversity indices. The results reveal a balanced distribution of supportive and opposing stances, yet a low diversity of argumentative frames. This pattern suggests that German media exhibited a liberal-aggregative model of diversity, emphasizing coexistence of opinions over deliberative engagement with competing interpretations. Despite frequent claims of uniform pro-government bias, our findings indicate that coverage was more heterogeneous than critics claimed. However, they also point to limited argumentative depth and a tendency to reproduce existing political logics. We discuss the methodological and normative challenges of quantifying diversity, particularly under conditions of war and uncertainty, and argue that criticism of media bias often reflects broader transformations in the perception of journalistic diversity.

item.title: Beyond Digital Access: Social Resilience to Political Misinformation in Rural Indonesia
item.dc:creator: Eko Bagus Sholihin, Yulion Zalpa, Wahyu Wulandari, Ainur Ropik, Ismail Alviano
item.description:
Political Communication · Eko Bagus Sholihin, Yulion Zalpa, Wahyu Wulandari, Ainur Ropik, Ismail Alviano

Topics: Political misinformation, Digital divide, Social capital, Political polarization

This article interrogates the information deficit model in studies of political misinformation by examining how a rural Indonesian community with recent and shallow digital connectivity responded to electoral misinformation during the 2024 presidential campaign. Digital divide scholarship assumes that limited access and skills leave rural populations vulnerable to misinformation and reliant on external intervention. Drawing on a survey (n = 400), 20 interviews, and field and digital observation in the transmigrant communities of the Banyuasin waterways, where mobile internet arrived only in late 2019, we find a different pattern. Although residents rely heavily on social media they distrust for electoral information, a large majority neither forwarded nor amplified political content, and recorded disputes were absent during the period observed. We identify three socio-cultural mechanisms that account for this: bonding social capital that embeds information evaluation in dense face-to-face networks; partisan identity that, under conditions of economic interdependence, is expressed through restraint rather than confrontation; and dual-sphere norms that separate offline political talk from a deliberately quiet online presence. We argue that these mechanisms produce social resilience – the community absorbs false claims without fracturing – but that this is distinct from, and costly to, democratic vitality: the same practices that limit the circulation of misinformation also limit its correction and mute those least embedded in local networks. Theoretically, the relationship between digital access, skill, and democratic outcomes is not merely non-linear but differently specified: communities may be socially resilient to misinformation without being epistemically resilient to it. Empirically, the study offers rare micro-level evidence from rural Southeast Asia. Practically, it cautions against reading the absence of visible conflict as evidence that a community is managing information well.

item.title: Emotion Regulation of Fear in Children’s TV Series: An Exploratory Analysis of Media Portrayals
item.dc:creator: Steven Stelz, Jennifer Krol, Katharina Savu, Stefanie M. Jungmann
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Steven Stelz, Jennifer Krol, Katharina Savu, Stefanie M. Jungmann

Topics: Emotion regulation, Media portrayals, Children's television, Fear

Audiovisual media may provide young children with models of fear regulation. However, little is known about how characters in children’s television respond to fear and which regulatory strategies are portrayed. This study examined emotion regulation in 35 fear-related scenes from 12 television series popular among preschool-aged children, rated by 45 independent raters. The scenes were systematically evaluated regarding the regulatory strategies displayed by the characters, their adaptiveness, and the intensity of the depicted fear. Problem-oriented action (71.1%) and withdrawal (60.4%) were most frequently depicted. Higher fear intensity was associated with greater withdrawal (ρ = .65, p < .001). Adaptive regulation predominated overall (70.4%; p = .001), whereas avoidance did not predominate over confrontation. No significant gender differences emerged. Overall, the findings indicate that children’s television portrays diverse regulatory responses to fear, with problem-oriented action and withdrawal being particularly prominent. These findings provide a foundation for future research examining how young children perceive and interpret these regulatory responses.

item.title: AI Chatbot’s Self-Confidence Cues Shape Users’ Impressions of the Chatbot, but Not Accuracy Judgments of Hallucinated Responses
item.dc:creator: Eun-Ju Lee, Jin Won Park, Sukyoung Choi, Sungwon Hwang
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Eun-Ju Lee, Jin Won Park, Sukyoung Choi, Sungwon Hwang

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Human-AI interaction, Information credibility, Source credibility

A 2 × 2 × 2 (confidence level × confidence variability × confidence modality) between-subjectsonline experiment (N = 738) examined how an AI chatbot’s self-confidence influences users’ evaluations of the chatbot and its hallucinated outputs. When confidence variability was low, more dominant participants evaluated the verbal (vs. numerical) chatbot more positively and indicated greater willingness to use it, whereas less dominant participants favored the numerical chatbot. In the high-variability condition, these patterns disappeared. Post-hoc analyses show that attributing greater dominance to a verbal chatbot triggered the similarity-attraction heuristic, but it did not affect users’ perceived accuracy of the chatbot’s outputs.

item.title: From Communication Anxiety to Psychological Reliance
item.dc:creator: Mina Choi, Hyesun Choung, Inyoung Shin, Samuel Hardman Taylor
item.description:
Journal of Media Psychology · Mina Choi, Hyesun Choung, Inyoung Shin, Samuel Hardman Taylor

Topics: Generative AI, Communication anxiety, Longitudinal study, Human-AI interaction

Abstract: Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study investigates how communication anxiety and psychological need satisfaction relate to the use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based chatbots, specifically ChatGPT, for communication tasks (e.g., writing emails, drafting messages, and preparing scripts). Using a three-wave panel survey of participants from the United States and South Korea, we examined both between- and within-person dynamics. Results showed that individuals with higher trait-level communication anxiety tended to use ChatGPT more frequently for communication tasks, whereas within-person fluctuations in anxiety did not predict greater use. ChatGPT use was positively associated with the satisfaction of basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence, and relatedness – and this need satisfaction, in turn, was associated with greater psychological reliance on ChatGPT. Importantly, need satisfaction further mediated the relationship between ChatGPT use and psychological reliance at both within- and between-person levels. Cultural comparisons revealed that US participants exhibited stronger momentary effects, while Korean participants showed more stable, trait-based patterns. These findings highlight the role of LLM-based chatbots as need-supportive communication tools that may become integrated into users’ communication practices over time, with implications for theories of AI-mediated communication, cross-cultural research, and the design of human-AI communication systems.

item.title: Testing the Parasocial Contact Hypothesis Through Stand-Up Comedy
item.dc:creator: John A. Banas, Elena Bessarabova, Doris E. Acheme, Valerie Biwa, Norman C. H. Wong
item.description:
Journal of Media Psychology · John A. Banas, Elena Bessarabova, Doris E. Acheme, Valerie Biwa, Norman C. H. Wong

Topics: Parasocial relationships, Media effects, Persuasion, Social identity

Abstract: The study examined how humorous parasocial contact can reduce prejudice toward outgroups. Study predictions were tested in an experiment ( N = 301) comparing the effects of a comedy stand-up by a Muslim comedian (Hasan Minhaj or Mohammed Amer) to a control condition a stand-up from a non-Muslim comedian (Brian Regan or Jim Gaffigan). Results indicated that humorous parasocial contact was effective at facilitating parasocial relationships in all conditions. Consistent with study predictions, when participants were exposed to the mediated intergroup contact with a Muslim comedian, parasocial relationships – mediated through intergroup anxiety – were positively associated with willingness for contacts with Muslims (i.e., negatively associated with social distance) and negatively associated with endorsement of Muslim stereotypes. In contrast, these mediational relationships were not observed when mediated intergroup contact occurred with a White comedian. These and other results are discussed along with implications, limitations, and future research directions.

item.title: Paid, but not a partner: Monetization without standing in Facebook’s Performance Bonus Program
item.dc:creator: Rebecca C. Hains
item.description:
New Media & Society · Rebecca C. Hains

Topics: Platform governance, Social media platforms, Digital labor, User-generated content

Platform revenue-sharing programs both pay and govern creators. Drawing on interviews with 18 participants in Facebook’s Performance Bonus Program (PBP) and the author’s own participation, this study examines how monetization reshaped creators’ platform governance expectations. PBP’s onboarding, which addressed recipients as “valued creators” and promised earnings of “up to $30,000 a month,” combined with early recurring payouts to cultivate expectations of continuity and institutional responsiveness, particularly among participants new to monetization. When enforcement errors, payout volatility, and support failures followed, participants discovered that payment had not conferred meaningful access to explanation, human review, or recourse. This article theorizes that condition as monetization without standing : a governance arrangement in which creators are compensated and governed as laborers while denied the procedural recognition typically associated with paid work. This arrangement constitutes a breach of the psychological contract generated by monetization, producing durable behavioral constraint, disparate impacts on marginalized creators, and creator attrition.

item.title: Ambivalence and antagonism: The intertwinement of gossiping and public shaming on social media
item.dc:creator: Hanna-Kaisa Lassila
item.description:
New Media & Society · Hanna-Kaisa Lassila

Topics: Social media, Online communities, Cyberbullying, Self-presentation

The vernacular practices of public shaming and gossiping on social media function both as entertainment and as disciplinary mechanisms. This article investigates two Finnish subreddits on Reddit, where gossiping and public shaming practices are closely intertwined. On these subreddits, screenshots of Finnish social media content creators’ posts are intensely circulated, scrutinised and dissected. This article examines how the gossiping practices are tied to the vernacular practices of public shaming on social media and what these practices are affixed to within the discourses created on these subreddits. The study found that the entertainment and judgement derived from these practices are tethered to themes of unpredictability, ambivalence and community building. These create moral discourses about non-normative ways of self-presentation and public conduct, both in corporal and online realms. Moreover, this study exemplifies that when gossiping and public shaming on social media intertwine, the line between disciplining and bullying becomes easier to cross.

item.title: Fuck You, Pay Me: Payment apps, review platforms, and ambivalent resistance in the influencer industry
item.dc:creator: Sarah Edwards
item.description:
New Media & Society · Sarah Edwards

Topics: Social media influencers, Platform governance, Digital labor, Social media platforms

This article critically examines emerging intermediaries in the influencer industry that aggregate anonymous reviews of brands and allow influencers to report how much they were paid. Turning to four intermediaries (Fuck You Pay Me, Willa, Hashtag Pay Me, and Clara for Creators), I argue that although these emerging intermediaries represent an important step toward creating more equity, these efforts are a double-edged sword and represent a form of ambivalent resistance to broader structures governing the influencer industry. While these intermediaries are used to resist the precarity of platformized and branded cultural production, these transactions have the potential to be co-opted—used for surveillance and data tracking by brands, platforms, and corporations—potentially blunting emerging forms of collective action and solidarity. Ultimately, these intermediaries provide an opportunity to theorize forms of resistance to precarity as neither “top-down” nor “bottom-up,” but rather a means of negotiating and navigating power from limited and precarious positions.

item.title: Negotiated autonomy: A typology of negotiation strategies in podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism in Turkey
item.dc:creator: Gizem Uyanık
item.description:
Journalism · Gizem Uyanık

Topics: Journalism, Digital journalism, Podcasts, Platform studies

This study examines how entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts negotiate neoliberal entrepreneurial demands within a precarious, platform-based media environment. Existing scholarship has conceptualized journalists’ responses to precarious and neoliberal labor conditions through concepts such as resistance, coping, and resilience. This study proposes negotiation as a distinct strategic response that captures how journalists selectively recalibrate the terms and boundaries of their engagement with structural demands through conditional acceptance, refusal, modification, and boundary-setting. The study is based on in-depth interviews with 10 entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts in Türkiye, with the interview data analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings identify four interrelated negotiation strategies embedded in the everyday production practices of podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism: ethical negotiation, temporal negotiation, visibility negotiation, and collective negotiation. These strategies respond respectively to neoliberal pressures associated with commercialization, continuous productivity, personal branding, and the individualization of labor; however, they remain constrained by financial precarity, platform visibility pressures, and fragile conditions of sustainability. The findings show that entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts selectively recalibrate the terms and boundaries of their engagement with neoliberal demands while remaining embedded within structural constraints and preserving limited spaces of professional autonomy. By conceptualizing negotiation as a distinct form of strategic response and identifying its four empirical forms, the study contributes a typology for explaining how bounded and provisional professional autonomy is produced under persistent structural constraints in podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism.

item.title: Prioritizing Journalistic Norms or Humanitarian Values? A Multistage Computational Analysis of Journalistic Role Performance in Humanitarian News
item.dc:creator: Zhe Xu, Martin Scott, Dani Madrid‐Morales, Kate Wright, Shuai Wang
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Zhe Xu, Martin Scott, Dani Madrid‐Morales, Kate Wright, Shuai Wang

Topics: Journalistic roles, Journalistic practice, Humanitarian journalism, Computational methods

This study examines how journalistic roles are performed in humanitarian news. Using a multistage computational approach applied to news data from 46 international news organizations across 21 countries, we find that role performance varies systematically across topics, political systems, and organizational types. Our findings complicate the predominant tendency in humanitarian journalism scholarship to frame roles in terms of professional norms or humanitarian values. Instead, we show that role performance is multidimensional and contextually contingent. Improving humanitarian coverage therefore requires attention not only to professional practices but also to the institutional conditions that enable diverse forms of journalism.

item.title: The Effects of Target Characteristics on Public Support for Hate Speech Laws
item.dc:creator: Jesper Sommer Rasmussen
item.description:
Political Communication · Jesper Sommer Rasmussen

Topics: Public opinion, Media effects, Persuasion, Social identity

Does the target of speech shape public support for hate speech laws? Regulating hate speech is controversial, partly because partisans are assumed to disagree over which groups such laws should protect. This article conducts a comprehensive test of how support for hate speech laws varies across partisan lines when speech targets ethnic, religious, gender, or political groups. Based on conjoint experiments in Denmark and the United States, the results show that support for regulation increases by up to 32% points when severity increases from “incivility” to “incitement to violence.” Target characteristics increase support for regulation by up to 6.3% points and exert the strongest effects when speech targets ethnic and religious groups rather than gender or political groups. These effects persist when severity is held constant and are broadly stable across severity levels. They are also heterogeneous across partisan groups, mostly ranging from 3 to 7.2% points, with one exception reaching 11.9% points. In neither country are partisans more willing to regulate hate speech targeting their political opponents than hate speech targeting their political allies. Overall, severity has the strongest effect on support for hate speech regulation, while target characteristics have smaller, heterogeneous effects that are largest when speech targets ethnic or religious groups.

item.title: When Epistemic Authority Collapses: Linking Fake News Media Perception and Conspiracy Beliefs to Disinformation Vulnerability
item.dc:creator: Alberto Ardèvol‐Abreu, Alberto E. López-Carrión, Jenny del Pino García Sánchez
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Alberto Ardèvol‐Abreu, Alberto E. López-Carrión, Jenny del Pino García Sánchez

Topics: Disinformation, Conspiracy theories, Fake news, Misinformation

Citizens increasingly need to detect and filter disinformation, yet we know little about why some are more vulnerable than others. We examine whether forms of skepticism toward traditional epistemic authorities—fake news media perception (FNMP) and conspiracy beliefs—are associated with disinformation vulnerability. Using two-wave survey data from Spain ( N W1 = 1,207; n W2 = 821), we find that FNMP is widespread, not a fringe phenomenon. Conspiracy beliefs predict vulnerability across cross-sectional, lagged, and autoregressive models. Support for FNMP as a predictor is partial and not sustained in autoregressive models. Evidence for the interaction between FNMP and conspiracy beliefs is weak.

item.title: TikTok News: How The Washington Post ’s Use of Platform Logics Affects Perceptions of Journalists and News Learning
item.dc:creator: Audrey Halversen, Brian E. Weeks
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Audrey Halversen, Brian E. Weeks

Topics: TikTok, Platform affordances, Journalism, Media trust

In a period of high competition, many contemporary journalists attract audience attention by adopting the stylistic conventions (“logics”) of platforms like TikTok to deliver news online. However, the effects of this content on audience trust and learning remain unclear. Using two online experiments, we examine whether audiences perceive journalists as credible and learn from news videos employing TikTok logics, compared to traditional print articles. Results indicate that journalists using TikTok logics may effectively capture attention but are viewed as less trustworthy, credible, professional, and knowledgeable, though more likable, than print journalists. Learning outcomes are similar across formats.

item.title: Cue production and evaluative uptake: prompt framing and user judgments in AI-Mediated health communication
item.dc:creator: Zhan Xu, Hao Guo
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Zhan Xu, Hao Guo

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Health communication, Source credibility, Human-AI interaction

Conversational AI systems are increasingly embedded in everyday information and support-seeking practices, including health-related interactions in which users seek advice, reassurance, or emotional acknowledgment. Yet less is known about how users’ own communicative framing shapes what AI systems produce, and whether such AI-generated emotional and supportive cues are subsequently taken up in users’ evaluations of the interaction. Drawing on research on human-like social cues and cue-based credibility processing, this study distinguishes between cue production and cue uptake in AI-mediated communication. Using a randomized, naturalistic prompt-based experiment, participants engaged in a brief two-turn exchange with ChatGPT using one of three prompt exemplars about sleep difficulty that varied in solution orientation, distress expression, and help-seeking structure. The study combined experimental manipulation, computational analysis of AI-generated responses, and pre–post measures of perceived emotional understanding, credibility, trust, and intended future use. Prompt framing shaped the emotional and supportive cues of AI responses: distress-expressive prompts elicited higher anxiety-related language scores, solution-oriented prompts produced more positive emotional tone, and mixed help-seeking prompts elicited more reassuring language. However, variation in these features was not reliably associated with differential pre–post changes in users’ evaluations. Across conditions, users reported modest increases in perceived emotional understanding, credibility, and intended future use after the interaction. The findings suggest that conversational AI can adapt its language to users’ framing, but such cue production does not necessarily lead to credibility uptake. The study contributes to research on AI-mediated communication by examining emotional cueing in a live, ecologically realistic interaction context.

item.title: The integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring: a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ hate speech
item.dc:creator: John Patrick Crowley, Elizabeth A. Hintz, Amanda Denes
item.description:
Journal of Communication · John Patrick Crowley, Elizabeth A. Hintz, Amanda Denes

Topics: Social support, Interpersonal communication, Online harassment, Communication theory

Abstract Social support is a fundamental human need and communication process. Yet, scholars theorizing about social support have been limited by several pervasive assumptions: (a) people are able to recruit support when needed, (b) others are willing and able to provide support, (c) what counts as “good” support is mutually understood and desirable, and (d) support seeking is binary and static. Researchers must productively move beyond these assumptions to enhance the depth and breadth of theorizing about the process of support seeking. By addressing these assumptions and consolidating the literature concerning support seeking and marshaling, we set forth the novel, field-general integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring (ITSNS) grounded in the interpretive paradigm. To accomplish this, we introduce process theorizing, forward three propositions forming the ITSNS’ heuristic framework, and offer criteria for evaluating the ITSNS. Finally, to illustrate the utility of the ITSNS in research practice, we offer a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ people seeking support following an experience of hate speech.

item.title: Flooding the zone during the 2026 war on Iran: Coverage of the Minab School attack in US and UK media
item.dc:creator: Kareem El Damanhoury, Abeer Al-Najjar
item.description:
Journalism · Kareem El Damanhoury, Abeer Al-Najjar

Topics: Journalism, Media framing, News coverage, Political communication

In the age of disinformation, “flooding the zone” has hardened from a campaign tactic into a condition of war. The bombing of a girls’ school in Minab on the first day of the US-Israeli campaign on Iran and President Trump’s insistence that Iran, or somebody else, bore responsibility provide a critical case study to understand journalistic practices in such context. Using quantitative content and qualitative framing analyses, the study examines the level of attention to the Minab school attack in US and UK news media and its coverage in eight American and British publications—New York Times, Washington Post, Wall Street Journal, New York Post, Guardian, Daily Mirror, Daily Mail, and the Sun—in the first month to compare reporting patterns, sourcing, blaming attribution, and lexicalization by country and political leaning. The findings reveal a departure from the traditional news cycle in US and UK media’s coverage of the Minab school attack, a prioritization of accountability narratives and human interest reporting over the humanitarian fallout, and a structural lag that reproduces the slow, source-licensed concession of home-state responsibility that Herman and Chomsky's propaganda model predicts. The reporting patterns further reveal a problematic relegation of Iranian civilian voices in covering a mass civilian casualty event that directly affected them. The study concludes with a discussion of the grievable versus ungrievable children in Western media and the implications of such dynamics for the study of children as casualties of conflict and for the ethics of war reporting in flooded zones.

item.title: Differentiating authority in hydrogen news: Source hierarchies and evaluative positions across Germany and MENA newspapers
item.dc:creator: Majid Ali, Lutz M. Hagen
item.description:
Journalism · Majid Ali, Lutz M. Hagen

Topics: News sourcing, Source credibility, Science journalism, Media framing

News sourcing research establishes institutional dominance, yet broad measures of elite visibility obscure how authority shapes access and evaluation. Using the HOI model, this study compares the attributed visibility and evaluative positions of political, economic, epistemic, international, civil society, lay-public, and journalistic actors in hydrogen coverage. A quantitative content analysis examined over 16,000 attributed statements in newspapers from Germany, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Egypt. Political and economic actors dominated external visibility; epistemic and international actors were secondary, while civil society and lay-public voices remained marginal. Political and international actors expressed the most positive evaluations, whereas epistemic actors and journalists were more cautious. German coverage exhibited greater differentiation in actor-linked evaluations, while MENA newspapers displayed more uniformly affirmative positions across actors. The findings demonstrate that institutional dominance varies in composition and evaluative implications across contexts.

item.title: Perceived Sources Matter: Implications of Misinformation on Media Trust and News Avoidance Under Different Levels of Press Freedom
item.dc:creator: Yuteng Zheng, Michael Chan, Francis Lap Fung Lee
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Yuteng Zheng, Michael Chan, Francis Lap Fung Lee

Topics: Misinformation, Media trust, News avoidance, Press freedom

Extant research on the impact of misinformation on media trust and news avoidance behavior has produced competing arguments and findings. The present study argues that the relationships among misinformation, media trust, and news avoidance can be better specified by considering whether people perceive misinformation as coming primarily from established institutions or non-institutional sources. Given the close linkage between the mainstream news media and established social and political institutions, people are likely to exhibit lower levels of news trust and higher levels of news avoidance if they perceive misinformation as coming from institutional sources. In contrast, when people perceive misinformation as coming from non-institutional sources, they may rely on the news media as authoritative fact-checkers and hence trust the news more and avoid it less. Societal-level press freedom is likely to moderate such relationships. The arguments and hypotheses are tested by an analysis of Digital News Report 2025 data.

item.title: Extending the Deservingness Framework to Communication Sciences
item.dc:creator: David De Coninck, Lise-Lore Steeman
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · David De Coninck, Lise-Lore Steeman

Topics: Media framing, Content analysis, Journalism, Political communication

While communication research has documented how media frame social groups as victims or threats, little is known about the evaluative criteria through which mediated discourse constructs minority representations. This study introduces deservingness as a framework for analyzing such evaluative logics, drawing on the Control, Attitude, Reciprocity, Identity, Need (CARIN) criteria. We illustrate this through an analysis of 7,561 Belgian newspaper articles across three migration contexts (2015, 2021, 2022), combining automated dictionary-based content analysis with a theory-driven qualitative content analysis of 284 articles. Results reveal a stable but context-sensitive deservingness communication. We position deservingness as a transferable tool for research on moral evaluation and conditional solidarity.

item.title: Islamophobia and Online News: Elite News Discourse and Comments About the Daegu Mosque in South Korea
item.dc:creator: David Chison Oh, Yoon Esther Lee
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · David Chison Oh, Yoon Esther Lee

Topics: Online news, News coverage, Media framing, Public opinion

In 2023, dozens of Daegu residents protested the construction of a mosque outside of the gates of Kyungpook National University. This article analyzes the discourse of news stories and reader comments in order to understand how the elite news discourse was contested by the popular discourse of a largely far-right comments space. The elite discourse in the newspaper articles normalized institutional authority and the projection of the nation as a liberal democratic actor while the comments articulated common tropes within global Islamophobia while also being grounded in specific local politics and nationalist identity construction set against the Muslim Other.

item.title: The making of cloud computing: an antecedent of scalability
item.dc:creator: Devika Narayan
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Devika Narayan

Topics: Digital infrastructure, Digital platforms, Platformization, Computational methods

This paper offers a historically situated analysis of cloud computing. Cloud computing is a paradigm for provisioning computing infrastructure that now has enormous reach. It is defined by its unique scalability. This unique scalability has proven to be enormously impactful in the digital economy and beyond, shaping the emergence of platform ecosystems, the development of AI, and the process of digitalization in the 21st century. As important as it is to grapple with this scalability, it is easy to reify. This paper examines emergent sociotechnical practices that sought to make the computer more flexible. The study focuses on specific efforts within the Research Department of a major US technology company. The analysis of scalability I offer is based on interviews with former engineers in this Lab as well as archival material. I trace projects and practices as teams forayed into making a relatively fixed machine more dynamic and more scalable. This paper advances emerging literatures on cloud computing and digital infrastructure by offering a grounded analysis of scalability-in-the-making.

item.title: Participation in the smart city: disability and autonomous public transport in Singapore
item.dc:creator: Wenqi Tan, Shirley S. Ho
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Wenqi Tan, Shirley S. Ho

Topics: Smart cities, Digital inequality, Qualitative content analysis, Media representation

Amidst the increasing interdependency between bodies and technology in smart city space, this article examines the extent to which disabled people can participate in the development and discursive construction of smart city technology. While citizen participation in urban planning and decision-making processes is ostensibly a key pillar of the smart city concept, the actual and meaningful capacity for citizens – especially disabled citizens – to translate their interests into smart city technology systems remains limited. In this article, we focus on the weaving of autonomous vehicle technology into Singapore’s city space as autonomous public transport is situated as an integral part of the country’s imagined future as a ‘driverless vehicle city.’ Findings from a qualitative content analysis of 86 newspaper articles about autonomous public transport, published from August 2013 to August 2025, and a series of online focus group discussions with 20 people with ambulatory disability indicate few opportunities for disabled people to democratically participate in autonomous public transport development and hold a stake in Singapore’s smart, driverless future, as well as a disappearance of disability from public communication about the technology.
